title: RUPlace: Optimizing Routability via Unified Placement and Routing Formulation
problem: Placement optimization in advanced VLSI designs struggles with routing congestion management; existing methods lack theoretical foundations and decouple placement from routing, missing optimization synergies.
method: ADMM-based placer that alternately optimizes global routing and incremental placement using Wasserstein distance and bilevel optimization. A convex programming model determines optimal cell inflation ratios for global placement while directly minimizing routed congestion.

title: ASDR: Exploiting Adaptive Sampling and Data Reuse for CIM-based Instant Neural Rendering
problem: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) inference exhibits irregular memory access patterns and high computational overhead, making it unsuitable for low-latency, power-efficient deployment on edge devices. Standard compute architectures cannot bridge the gap between NeRF's memory-bound irregular accesses and the immediacy/power requirements of practical neural rendering.
method: ASDR maps NeRF inference onto computing-in-memory (CIM) arrays to address the memory access bottleneck by performing computation near data storage, eliminating costly DRAM transfers. Adaptive sampling reduces the number of points sampled per ray dynamically based on scene complexity, cutting redundant computation. Data reuse strategies exploit spatial and temporal coherence across adjacent rays and frames to avoid redundant CIM macro activations. Together, these techniques reduce both the number of operations and the energy per operation on the CIM substrate.

title: Let-Me-In: (Still) Employing In-pointer Bounds Metadata for Fine-grained GPU Memory Safety
problem: GPU programs written in C/C++ inherit memory safety vulnerabilities such as out-of-bounds accesses. The heterogeneous GPU memory hierarchy (heap, local memory, thousands of concurrent threads) makes it difficult to enforce fine-grained bounds checking with low overhead.
method: LMI aligns GPU memory allocations to powers-of-two boundaries and performs static analysis at compile time to identify and mark pointer arithmetic instructions. Bounds metadata (base and size) is encoded into the unused upper bits of 64-bit GPU virtual address pointers, eliminating separate metadata memory structures. Hardware bounds-checking logic validates each memory access against the in-pointer metadata before issuing the request, adding minimal per-access latency even under thousands of concurrent threads.

title: Power-Constrained Printed Neuromorphic Hardware Training
problem: Printed neuromorphic circuits (pNCs) must operate under severe power budgets from printed batteries or energy harvesters while maintaining task accuracy; traditional penalty-based optimization requires hundreds of training runs to explore power-accuracy tradeoffs.
method: Augmented Lagrangian optimization enforces task-specific power constraints directly during training, computing optimal power-accuracy tradeoffs in a single run. Tested across 13 benchmarks with different activation functions (p-tanh, p-Clipped_ReLU).

title: Dynamic Partial Deadlock Detection and Recovery via Garbage Collection
problem: Concurrent message-passing programs in Go are susceptible to partial deadlocks where goroutines block indefinitely on channels, causing severe memory leaks in long-running systems. Existing techniques cannot both detect and automatically recover from these partial deadlocks at runtime.
method: GOLF extends Go's garbage collector marking phase to soundly approximate goroutine liveness: a goroutine is considered live only if its channel references are reachable from the GC root set. During GC marking, goroutines blocked on channels with no live senders are flagged as deadlocked. Detected deadlocked goroutines are then automatically cancelled or cleaned up to free memory and restore system progress. The detection integrates directly into the existing GC pause with minimal overhead.

title: CognitiveArm: Enabling Real-Time EEG-Controlled Prosthetic Arm Using Embodied Machine Learning
problem: Real-time EEG processing for brain-controlled prosthetics requires efficient on-device inference (filtering, feature extraction, classification) while maintaining low latency and high accuracy on resource-constrained edge hardware.
method: CognitiveArm system integrates BrainFlow EEG library with optimized deep learning models. Uses evolutionary search for Pareto-optimal DL configs via hyperparameter tuning, optimizer analysis, window selection, and ensemble combinations. Model compression (pruning/quantization) optimizes for embedded deployment. Voice commands enable mode switching.

title: Vela: A Virtualized LLM Training System with GPU Direct RoCE
problem: LLM training at scale typically requires dedicated bare-metal GPU clusters with specialized interconnects (InfiniBand, NVLink), but deploying LLM training on cloud-native virtualized infrastructure using commodity hardware and standard Ethernet-based RDMA (RoCE) introduces performance challenges from virtualization overhead and suboptimal network stack interactions.
method: Vela uses Linux KVM-based virtualization with SRIOV-based network interfaces to enable GPU-to-GPU peer-to-peer DMA (GPU Direct) across VMs without passing through the host CPU. VMs are connected via a virtualized RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) network built from off-the-shelf NICs. The system was deployed on NVIDIA A100 GPUs in IBM Cloud, using model parallelism for a 50B-parameter decoder model at ~1500 GPU scale, and insights from 2.5 years of production operation guide architectural recommendations.

title: 3D-CIMlet: A Chiplet Co-Design Framework for Heterogeneous In-Memory Acceleration of Edge LLM Inference and Continual Learning
problem: Edge AI hardware supporting both LLM inference and continual learning remains underexplored; 2D chiplet designs incur thermal and energy inefficiencies when integrating diverse memory technologies (RRAM, eDRAM) for accelerated inference.
method: 3D-CIMlet uses memory-reliability-aware chiplet mapping strategies across 2.5D/3D heterogeneous CIM chiplet architectures combining RRAM, capacitor-less eDRAM, and hybrid chiplets in mixed technology nodes, with thermal modeling to optimize placement for edge LLM tasks.

title: Early Termination for Hyperdimensional Computing Using Inferential Statistics
problem: Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) inference can be terminated early to reduce computation, but existing heuristic early-termination methods lack statistical guarantees and may either unacceptably degrade classification accuracy or terminate inference later than necessary. There is no principled, statistically grounded method for HDC early termination.
method: The paper applies inferential statistics (hypothesis testing) to HDC classification to derive a principled early-termination criterion. Rather than using a heuristic threshold, it formulates the termination decision as a statistical test on the similarity scores of HDC class hypervectors, computing confidence bounds and stopping inference when the test rejects ambiguity with the required statistical confidence. This allows provable accuracy-loss bounds while minimizing wasted computation.

title: Light-weight Cache Replacement for Instruction Heavy Workloads
problem: Modern instruction-heavy workloads (e.g., server-side software with large code footprints) place heavy pressure on the last-level cache (LLC), and state-of-the-art LLC replacement policies designed for general workloads impose high hardware overhead yet provide little additional benefit over simple policies when aggressive prefetching is also present. Existing policies such as Mockingjay require complex prediction infrastructure that is not justified by their marginal gains for instruction-heavy access patterns.
method: PACIPV (Prefetch-Aware Coarse-grained Insertion and Promotion Vectors) generalizes the Re-Reference Interval Prediction (RRIP) framework by parameterizing cache line insertion position and promotion position as configurable vectors rather than fixed rules. The design space of valid RRIP-based policies is enumerated exhaustively on a training workload set to find the optimal insertion and promotion vectors. The selected policy is prefetch-aware, distinguishing demand and prefetch accesses and assigning them different insertion/promotion behavior to prevent prefetch thrashing. The resulting hardware implementation uses simple counter logic with negligible area overhead compared to RRIP.

title: Transitive Array: An Efficient GEMM Accelerator with Result Reuse
problem: General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) in DNNs and LLMs incurs high computational cost and memory bandwidth demand, especially in resource-constrained deployments. Existing quantization and sparsity methods reduce precision but do not exploit reusable intermediate partial results within GEMM computation.
method: The paper introduces transitive sparsity, a novel paradigm where previously computed GEMM results are reused transitively via directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) that encode reuse relationships between partial products. An optimal DAG execution order is determined to resolve dependency and parallelism constraints. The Transitive Array accelerator exploits this sparsity through a multiplication-free design that distributes work across multiple parallel lanes for balanced throughput.

title: Relax: Composable Abstractions for End-to-End Dynamic Machine Learning
problem: Dynamic shape computations in modern ML workloads (especially LLMs) cannot be efficiently compiled by existing frameworks that treat computational graphs, loop-level tensor programs, and external library calls as separate, non-interoperable abstractions, preventing cross-level optimization and limiting deployment to diverse backends.
method: Relax introduces a unified compiler IR with a cross-level abstraction that encapsulates computational graphs, loop-level TIR (tensor IR) programs, and external library calls in a single representation. First-class symbolic shape annotations propagate dynamic shape information globally across the program, enabling shape-aware optimizations across abstraction levels. Relax builds an end-to-end compilation pipeline in Apache TVM that includes shape-aware kernel fusion, operator specialization, and deployment code generation for diverse targets including GPUs, mobile (Android/iOS), embedded MCUs, and WebAssembly/WebGPU.

title: Voyager: Input-Adaptive Algebraic Transformations for High-Performance Graph Neural Networks
problem: GNN execution performance is bottlenecked by irregular memory access patterns and low compute utilization, and algebraic transformations (operator reordering, operator fusion) that work well for dense DNNs fail to generalize across diverse and dynamically varying graph structures. Existing transformation strategies are applied statically and cannot adapt to per-input graph topology variations.
method: Voyager applies input-adaptive algebraic transformations that select or compose operator reordering and fusion strategies at runtime based on the structural properties of the incoming graph (e.g., degree distribution, density, sparsity patterns). It profiles lightweight graph statistics to guide transformation selection and generates optimized execution plans per input, avoiding the single static plan that prior compilers assume.

title: Reload+Reload: Exploiting Cache and Memory Contention Side Channel on AMD SEV
problem: AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) is designed to protect guest VMs in multi-tenant clouds via memory encryption, but two previously unknown side channels—cache flush timing and memory contention—expose information even through the SEV-SNP isolation boundary.
method: The authors discover and formalize two AMD-specific side channels: (1) a cache flush side channel exploitable via flush-set timing (RRFS), and (2) a memory contention side channel (RRMB). They construct two Reload+Reload attack variants that exploit these channels to observe memory access patterns without relying on the disabled Flush+Reload primitive. RRFS is used to build a covert channel for a Spectre attack; RRMB is used for AES-128 key extraction by timing memory block contention across VM boundaries under SEV-SNP.

title: Controlled Preemption: Amplifying Side-Channel Attacks from Userspace
problem: Many microarchitectural side-channel attacks are hampered by low temporal resolution measurements, which can preclude or significantly complicate extraction of sensitive information. Userspace attackers lack a mechanism to synchronize their observations with victim activity at fine-grained time resolution.
method: The paper introduces controlled preemption, a technique that allows a userspace attacker to precisely manipulate OS preemption timing in order to achieve fine-grained, synchronized measurement of victim microarchitectural state. By forcing preemption at attacker-chosen moments, the technique amplifies the signal quality of side-channel observations without requiring privileged access or hardware modifications.

title: Optimizing Deep Learning Inference Efficiency through Block Dependency Analysis
problem: ML compilers perform data dependency analysis at element or operator granularity, which creates overly complex inter-operator dependencies that block efficient fusion and overlap, and obscures parallelizable computation opportunities, leaving significant GPU utilization on the table.
method: BlockDepend introduces a block-level dependency analysis framework in the ML compiler pipeline. By operating at the level of tile/block computations (below operator level but above scalar element level), it extracts simplified dependency relationships between operators and identifies previously hidden parallelizable computation pairs. These dependencies drive targeted inter-operator memory access optimizations (e.g., producer-consumer fusion, shared memory reuse) and expose additional kernel-level parallelism that can be scheduled concurrently on GPU compute units.
